periods.activity_title: Idli-Vada: Counting Into Common Multiples

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Idli-Vada Game), section 5.1 p.107
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students sit in a circle and count aloud; they replace multiples of 3 with 'idli', multiples of 5 with 'vada', and common multiples of both with 'idli-vada'. Players who make a mistake are eliminated. Builds intuition for common multiples through a social game.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: At what number is 'idli-vada' said for the 10th time? (Find the 10th common multiple of 3 and 5.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: If the game is played from 1 to 90, find: (a) how many times 'idli' is said (including 'idli-vada'); (b) how many times 'vada' is said (including 'idli-vada'); (c) how many times 'idli-vada' is said.

time_bands.activity: Launch the game: arrange students in a circle and run Activity (Idli-Vada Game), section 5.1 p.107 ("students replace multiples of 3 with 'idli', multiples of 5 with 'vada'…."). Play one full round, with the teacher noting on the board every number called 'idli-vada'.

Pause the game and examine the board list together. Ask: what do these 'idli-vada' numbers have in common? Guide students to articulate that each is a multiple of both 3 and 5, naming these common multiples. Sketch a simple two-circle Venn diagram on the board, placing the common multiples in the overlap to anchor the vocabulary.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108 ("at what number is 'idli-vada' said for the 10th time?…") and Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.108 ("if the game is played from 1 to 90, how many times is 'idli' said?…"). Circulate and prompt students to list multiples systematically rather than continuing the game count.

Whole-class discussion of Q1 and Q2 answers. Draw out the observation that common multiples of 3 and 5 appear at regular intervals (every 15 numbers) and invite students to conjecture why — that 15 is the smallest such number. Collect conjectures without resolving them formally.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse multiples of 3, multiples of 5, and multiples of both — watch for those who list 15, 30, 45 for 'idli' rather than only for 'idli-vada'. The Venn diagram on the board serves as a persistent visual reference for the language of common multiples that the exercises in Q1 and Q2 then apply.

periods.activity_title: Venn Diagrams and Multiples: Seeing the Pattern

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is Fig. 5.1 (Venn diagram of multiples of 3 and 5) related to the Idli-Vada game? Draw the figure if the game is played till 60.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: Play the Idli-Vada game with different number pairs — (a) 2 and 5, (b) 3 and 7, (c) 4 and 6 — and draw Venn diagrams like Fig. 5.1 for each pair up to 60.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: What if the game was played till 900? How would the answers to Q2 change?

time_bands.activity: Recall that the Idli-Vada game with 3 and 5 produces common multiples at every 15th number. Students open their books to Fig. 5.1 and work on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.108 ("is Fig. 5.1 related to the Idli-Vada game? Draw the figure if the game is played till 60…."), sketching the Venn diagram in their notebooks.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.108 ("play the Idli-Vada game with different number pairs — (a) 2 and 5, (b) 3 and 7, (c) 4 and 6 — and draw Venn diagrams…."). Encourage them to write the common multiples in the overlap and compare diagrams with a neighbour.

Class discussion: compare the three Venn diagrams. Ask — where the overlap fills up quickly versus slowly, does the smallest common multiple reveal a pattern? Introduce the phrase 'least common multiple' descriptively. Then students attempt Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.108 ("what if the game was played till 900? How would the answers to Q2 change?…") using the patterns they identified.

Quick oral consolidation: each student states one observation from the three Venn diagrams in their own words. Teacher records key statements on the board and highlights that common multiples of two numbers repeat in a predictable pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: The pair (4, 6) in Q5 produces a notably denser overlap than (3, 7) — students who spot this are noticing that 4 and 6 share a common factor, an idea that will become central in section 5.3. Watch for students who place numbers that are multiples of only one number into the overlap region of the Venn diagram.

periods.activity_title: Jump Jackpot: Finding Common Factors Through Play

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Jump Jackpot), section 5.1 p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Grumpy places treasures on two numbers; Jumpy selects a jump size and can only land on multiples of that size. Students explore which jump sizes reach both treasure numbers, connecting common factors to a game mechanic.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Jump Jackpot, treasures are on 28 and 70. What jump sizes land on both numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.110
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find all multiples of 40 that lie between 310 and 410.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Activity (Jump Jackpot), section 5.1 p.109 ("Grumpy places treasures on two numbers; Jumpy selects a jump size and can only land on multiples of that size…."). With the class, place treasures on 12 and 18 and try jump sizes of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 — recording on the board which jump sizes reach both.

Pairs play the game with teacher-chosen treasure pairs (e.g., 20 and 30; 15 and 25) and list every successful jump size for each pair. After playing, each pair writes out all factors of each treasure number and circles the ones that appear in both lists — defining common factors through the game context.

Students solve Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.111 ("in Jump Jackpot, treasures are on 28 and 70. What jump sizes land on both numbers?…") independently. Then attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.110 ("find all multiples of 40 that lie between 310 and 410….") as a brief application of the multiple-scanning strategy.

Whole-class debrief: which jump size landed on both 28 and 70 but no larger jump size could? Connect this to the vocabulary 'greatest common factor'. Ask students: how is the greatest common factor related to all the common factors you listed?

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'factors of a number' with 'multiples of a number' when the game reverses direction from the Idli-Vada game; ask a few students to explain in their own words why a jump size must divide both treasures rather than be divisible by them. Having students list all factors systematically before identifying common ones prevents guess-and-check approaches that miss some common factors.

periods.activity_title: Reconstructing Venn Diagrams and Solving Factor Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors of: (a) 20 and 28; (b) 35 and 50; (c) 4, 8 and 12; (d) 5, 15 and 25.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Guna erased numbers from a Venn diagram leaving only the common multiples 24, 48, 72. Find possible values for the two circle labels (the individual multiples regions).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Anshu plays Idli-Vada with two numbers both smaller than 10. The first 'idli-vada' comes after number 50. What could the two numbers be?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: One number in an Idli-Vada game was 4 and nobody ever said just 'vada'. Which of 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 could be the other number?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.111
homework.description: A perfect number equals the sum of all its factors divided by 2. Given that 28 is perfect, find a perfect number between 1 and 10.

time_bands.activity: Students work independently on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.111 ("find the common factors of: (a) 20 and 28; (b) 35 and 50; (c) 4, 8 and 12; (d) 5, 15 and 25…."), listing all factors before identifying the common ones. Teacher circulates to check factor lists for completeness.

Introduce Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.111 ("Guna erased numbers from a Venn diagram leaving only the common multiples 24, 48, 72. Find possible values for the two circle labels….") as a reverse-engineering challenge. Students work in pairs, reasoning backwards from the common multiples to identify what the two circle numbers could be, recording multiple valid answers.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.111 ("Anshu plays Idli-Vada with two numbers both smaller than 10; the first 'idli-vada' comes after number 50….") and Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.108 ("one number in an Idli-Vada game was 4 and nobody ever said just 'vada'…."). These constraint-satisfaction problems reward systematic listing.

Share solutions to the reverse Venn diagram problem (Q8) — different pairs may have found different valid circle labels. Discuss how many correct answers exist and why, reinforcing that common multiples determine the structure of both circles.

periods.teacher_notes: Figure it Out Q8 has multiple valid answers — pairs who find only one should be prompted to look for others. A common error in Q4 is stopping after finding one or two common factors; encourage students to write every factor of each number before comparing lists.

periods.activity_title: Rectangles, Rows, and the Definition of Prime

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any even prime other than 2?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of the following numbers are prime: 23, 51, 37, 26?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify whether each statement is true or false and explain: (a) no prime has units digit 4; (b) a product of primes can be prime; (c) primes have no factors; (d) all even numbers are composite; (e) for every prime other than 2, the next number is composite.

time_bands.activity: Pose the rectangle-arrangement problem from the section narrative: students try to arrange 12 square tiles into as many different rectangles as possible (record dimensions on the board), then try the same with 7 tiles. Ask: what makes 7 different? Students articulate that 7 allows only a 1 × 7 arrangement because it has exactly two factors, while 12 has more.

From the tile exploration, introduce the definitions: a prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself); a composite number has more than two factors; and 1 is neither. Students classify each number from 2 to 20 as prime, composite, or neither in a table in their notebooks.

Students answer Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.114 ("is there any even prime other than 2?…") and Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.114 ("which of the following numbers are prime: 23, 51, 37, 26?…") — applying the definition they just built.

Class works through Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.114 ("identify whether each statement is true or false and explain….") together, with students giving verbal justifications before writing. Emphasise the statement about 1: students who classify 1 as prime should articulate why the definition of exactly two factors excludes it.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is classifying 1 as prime; anchor the definition firmly — exactly two distinct factors, 1 and itself — so students can self-check. For Q9(c), students often interpret 'no factors' literally; redirect them to the definition and ask how many factors 2 has.
materials: Square tiles or grid paper for tile arrangements

periods.activity_title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes: Uncovering All Primes to 100

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Are there an equal number of primes in every row of the sieve table? Which decades have the fewest primes? Which have the most?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the list of primes up to 100, what is the smallest difference between two successive primes? What is the largest difference?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Twin primes differ by 2. Find all twin prime pairs between 1 and 100.

time_bands.activity: Briefly recap that primes have exactly two factors. Ask: if you needed to find all primes up to 100, how would you do it systematically? Collect two or three student strategies, then announce that a method from about 2,200 years ago does this elegantly.

Students follow the Sieve of Eratosthenes procedure from section 5.2 on a printed or hand-drawn 10 × 10 grid: circle 2 and cross out all multiples of 2; circle 3 and cross out all multiples of 3 not already crossed; continue with 5, 7. The teacher models the first step on the board, then students complete the sieve independently. As they work, the teacher asks: why do we not need to check multiples of 11 for a grid up to 100?

Students use their completed sieve to answer Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.114 ("are there an equal number of primes in every row?…") and Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.114 ("what is the smallest difference between two successive primes? What is the largest?…"). Prompt students to record their row-by-row prime counts before drawing conclusions.

Students solve Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.114 ("twin primes differ by 2; find all twin prime pairs between 1 and 100….") using their sieve. Share findings as a class and introduce the term 'twin primes' formally.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes cross out 2 itself when striking multiples of 2 — remind them that the circled number is prime and only its proper multiples (from 2×2 onward) are struck. The question about why checking primes beyond 7 is unnecessary for a 100-grid (since 11² = 121 > 100) is a rich reasoning moment worth pausing on if students engage.
materials: Pencils or coloured pens for circling and crossing

periods.activity_title: Reasoning About Primes: Patterns, Proofs, and Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find seven consecutive composite numbers between 1 and 100.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write three pairs of prime numbers less than 20 whose sum is a multiple of 5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: 3 is prime and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also prime. Find at least five other primes p for which 2p + 1 is also prime.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.2 p.114
homework.description: The numbers 13 and 31 are prime and use the same digits. Find other such digit-reversal prime pairs up to 100.

time_bands.activity: Begin with Figure it Out Q7, section 5.2 p.114 ("find seven consecutive composite numbers between 1 and 100…."). Ask students to reason first: between which kinds of primes could a long composite run hide? Students work individually, then share methods — systematic listing from sieve versus conjectured gaps.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 5.2 p.114 ("write three pairs of prime numbers less than 20 whose sum is a multiple of 5….") and Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115 ("which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers?…"). For Q10, the reasoning must include partial factorisation — the teacher asks why guessing is insufficient.

Students explore Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115 ("3 is prime and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also prime; find at least five other primes p for which 2p + 1 is also prime….") — a conjecture-testing exercise. Pairs record their trials and share which values work and which do not.

Class debrief on Q12: are there patterns in which primes p make 2p + 1 also prime? Students pose conjectures aloud; teacher notes them on the board without resolving them — modelling that open questions are part of mathematics.

periods.teacher_notes: For Q10, students may try to identify the product by multiplying random triples of primes; encourage them instead to begin by factorising each candidate — connecting the exercise to the prime factorisation work that section 5.4 will formalise. Q12 is intentionally open-ended, so resist the urge to verify every student answer centrally; the habit of checking a conjecture against several cases is the learning goal.
materials: Completed sieve from the previous unit's work (or a fresh grid)

periods.activity_title: Safe Pairs: Introducing Co-prime Numbers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.3 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if each pair is 'safe' (co-prime): (a) 15 and 39; (b) 4 and 15; (c) 18 and 29; (d) 20 and 55.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of the following pairs are co-prime: (a) 18 and 35; (b) 15 and 37; (c) 30 and 415; (d) 17 and 69; (e) 81 and 18?

time_bands.activity: Re-enter the Jump Jackpot world from section 5.1: Grumpy now forbids jump size 1 and places treasures on 15 and 39. Ask the class — can Jumpy reach both? Students list common factors of 15 and 39, find that 3 is one, and conclude the treasures are reachable (not safe). Now try 4 and 15 — students list factors of each and find the only common factor is 1, so no jump size greater than 1 works. Introduce the term 'co-prime' for pairs whose only common factor is 1.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 5.3 p.115 ("check if each pair is 'safe' (co-prime): (a) 15 and 39; (b) 4 and 15; (c) 18 and 29; (d) 20 and 55….") by listing all factors of each number and identifying the common ones. Encourage them to check their answers against the opening examples.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 5.3 p.116 ("which of the following pairs are co-prime: (a) 18 and 35; (b) 15 and 37; (c) 30 and 415; (d) 17 and 69; (e) 81 and 18?…"). For larger numbers, prompt students to think about what factors to check systematically rather than listing all factors.
Class discussion: can two even numbers ever be co-prime? Can two prime numbers be co-prime? Students reason aloud using the definition (only common factor is 1) and the examples they just computed.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is assuming that two large numbers cannot be co-prime because they 'must share something' — the pair (17, 69) may surprise students since 69 = 3 × 23 shares no factor with 17. Encourage students who finish early to investigate whether a prime and any other number it does not divide are always co-prime.

periods.activity_title: Co-prime Art: Thread Diagrams and Pattern Prediction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Co-prime Art), section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students observe and analyse thread-art diagrams with different peg counts and thread-gaps. They predict which combinations visit all pegs (co-prime pairs) versus only some pegs (non-co-prime pairs) and create their own diagrams for four specified peg/gap combinations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find examples where the LCM equals the product of the two numbers, and examples where LCM is less than the product. How is this related to the pair being co-prime?

time_bands.activity: Show the thread-art diagrams from Activity (Co-prime Art), section 5.3 p.116 ("students observe and analyse thread-art diagrams with different peg counts and thread-gaps…."). Discuss the two examples in the book: ask students to count how many pegs are visited in each before predicting why one visits all pegs and one does not.

Students work on the four specified peg/gap combinations in Activity (Co-prime Art), section 5.3 p.116, drawing their own dot-and-line diagrams on paper. Before drawing each, they must write a prediction: will all pegs be visited? They check by finding whether the peg count and gap are co-prime.

Students engage with Math Talk, section 5.3 p.116 ("find examples where the LCM equals the product of the two numbers, and examples where LCM is less than the product; how is this related to the pair being co-prime?…"). They use small number pairs from their earlier factor work and the co-prime check to compile a table.

Brief gallery share: students hold up their thread diagrams and the class identifies whether they are co-prime patterns. Summarise the key observation: when peg count and gap are co-prime, the thread makes a single complete circuit visiting every peg exactly once.

periods.teacher_notes: The link between the LCM equalling the product and co-primality in the Math Talk is a conceptual high point: when two numbers share no common factor, their LCM is simply their product, which means the thread completes its circuit only after visiting every peg. Watch for students who predict 'all pegs visited' purely based on the gap being small rather than checking divisibility.
materials: Plain paper for drawing peg-and-thread diagrams

periods.activity_title: Why Ad Hoc Factorisation Fails: The Case for Prime Factorisation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.120
Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: A number's prime factorisation has one 2, two 3s, and one 11. What is the number?

time_bands.activity: Present the Anshu–Guna dialogue from section 5.4: Anshu writes 56 = 14 × 4 and concludes 56 and 63 share no common factor, but Guna shows 63 = 9 × 7 and 56 = 8 × 7, so 7 is common. Discuss: why did Anshu's approach fail? Lead students to see that partial factorisation does not guarantee all factors are visible. Introduce the tree diagram for 36 from the text, showing that different trees yield the same prime factors.

Model prime factorisation of 105 and 320 on the board using a factor tree, circling prime factors at each branch end. Emphasise that the final list contains only primes and the product of the list equals the original number. Students then tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.120 ("find the prime factorisations of: 64, 104, 105, 243, 320….") — selecting at least four numbers from the list.

Students solve Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.120 ("a number's prime factorisation has one 2, two 3s, and one 11; what is the number?…") — working backwards from prime factors to the number, which reverses and reinforces the factorisation process.

Whole-class check: two students share their factor trees for different numbers from Q1 on the board. Ask: did anyone start with a different first split but reach the same prime factors? Introduce the uniqueness principle — the set of prime factors is always the same regardless of how you begin the tree.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who start with the largest convenient factor tend to produce unbalanced trees but still arrive at the correct prime factorisation — affirm this and use it to motivate the uniqueness statement. The common error to watch for is leaving composite numbers (like 6 or 4) at branch ends without breaking them further.

periods.activity_title: Using Prime Factorisation to Check Co-primality

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Are the following pairs co-prime? Guess first, then verify using prime factorisation: (a) 30 and 45; (b) 57 and 85; (c) 121 and 1331; (d) 343 and 216.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Guna says any two prime numbers are co-prime. Is he right?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if 40 and 231 are co-prime using prime factorisation. 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 231 = 3 × 7 × 11 share no common prime factor; therefore 40 and 231 are co-prime.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 5.4 p.121
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if 242 and 195 are co-prime using prime factorisation. 242 = 2 × 11 × 11 and 195 = 3 × 5 × 13 share no common prime factor; therefore 242 and 195 are co-prime.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example, section 5.4 p.120 ("check if 40 and 231 are co-prime using prime factorisation; 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 231 = 3 × 7 × 11 share no common prime factor….") on the board. Then walk through Example, section 5.4 p.121 ("check if 242 and 195 are co-prime using prime factorisation; 242 = 2 × 11 × 11 and 195 = 3 × 5 × 13…."). Articulate the rule: compare prime factor lists — if the lists share no prime, the pair is co-prime.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.122 ("are the following pairs co-prime? Guess first, then verify using prime factorisation: (a) 30 and 45; (b) 57 and 85; (c) 121 and 1331; (d) 343 and 216…."). The instruction to guess before computing encourages reasoning before calculation.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.122 ("Guna says any two prime numbers are co-prime; is he right?…"). Students must construct an argument — listing a prime's factors (1 and itself) and showing that two distinct primes share no prime factor — rather than just verifying with examples.

Students share their argument for Q4. The class evaluates whether the argument is complete or relies on examples alone. Teacher clarifies that checking a few examples suggests but does not prove Guna's claim — the argument from the definition of prime does.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established co-primality by common-factor listing in section 5.3, students can now compare that method with the prime factorisation method and see why the latter is more reliable for larger numbers. Watch for students who write 121 = 11 × 11 but then incorrectly conclude it is prime because '11 is prime'.

periods.activity_title: Prime Factorisation Applied to Divisibility

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 5.4 p.121
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if 168 is divisible by 12. 168 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Since the prime factorisation of 12 is fully contained in that of 168 (168 = 12 × 14), 168 is divisible by 12.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if 42 is divisible by 12. 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. The prime factor 2 appears twice in 12 but only once in 42; therefore the prime factorisation of 12 is not included in that of 42, so 42 is not divisible by 12.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the first number divisible by the second? Use prime factorisation: (a) 225 and 27; (b) 96 and 24; (c) 343 and 17; (d) 999 and 99.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: First number has prime factorisation 2 × 3 × 7; second has 3 × 7 × 11. Are they co-prime? Does one divide the other?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.120
homework.description: Find the prime factorisation without multiplying first: (a) 56 × 25; (b) 108 × 75; (c) 1000 × 81.

time_bands.activity: Present Example, section 5.4 p.121 ("check if 168 is divisible by 12; 168 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3; since the prime factorisation of 12 is fully contained in that of 168….") and Example, section 5.4 p.122 ("check if 42 is divisible by 12; the prime factor 2 appears twice in 12 but only once in 42…."). Articulate the containment rule: divisor's prime factorisation must be fully included in the dividend's, counting multiplicity.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.122 ("is the first number divisible by the second? Use prime factorisation: (a) 225 and 27; (b) 96 and 24; (c) 343 and 17; (d) 999 and 99…."). Remind them to write full prime factorisations for both numbers before comparing.

Students solve Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.122 ("first number has prime factorisation 2 × 3 × 7; second has 3 × 7 × 11; are they co-prime? Does one divide the other?…"). This combines the co-primality check with the divisibility check in a single problem.

Quick oral summary: a student states in their own words the rule for divisibility by prime factorisation, and another student states the rule for co-primality. Teacher corrects any imprecision about counting prime factors with their multiplicity.

periods.teacher_notes: The multiplicity issue is the key difficulty: students may note that both 168 and 12 contain the prime 2 and conclude divisibility is confirmed — they must also verify that 2 appears at least as many times in 168 as in 12. For Q3, the pair is not co-prime (they share 3 and 7) and neither divides the other — students benefit from seeing that these two questions are independent.

periods.activity_title: Extended Prime Factorisation Practice and Number Construction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find three prime numbers, all less than 30, whose product is 1955.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the smallest number whose prime factorisation has: (a) three different prime numbers; (b) four different prime numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 5.4 p.121
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if 75 is divisible by 21. 75 = 3 × 5 × 5 and 21 = 3 × 7. Since 7 is a prime factor of 21 but not of 75, 75 is not divisible by 21.

time_bands.activity: Review Example, section 5.4 p.121 ("check if 75 is divisible by 21; 75 = 3 × 5 × 5 and 21 = 3 × 7; since 7 is a prime factor of 21 but not of 75….") as a quick warm-up, ensuring the containment rule is clear before moving to more open problems.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.120 ("find three prime numbers, all less than 30, whose product is 1955…."). Students must reason about which primes divide 1955, working systematically by trial with small primes. Encourage writing out the factorisation step by step.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 5.4 p.120 ("what is the smallest number whose prime factorisation has: (a) three different prime numbers; (b) four different prime numbers?…"). Pairs discuss strategy: to minimise the number, use the smallest available primes and each to the power of one.

Debrief Q5: students share their answers and reasoning. Ask: what if you needed five different prime factors — what is the smallest such number, and how big would it be? This open extension connects to the idea that primes are the atoms of multiplication.

periods.teacher_notes: For Q3, a useful entry point is checking whether 1955 is divisible by small primes in order (5 divides it immediately since the last digit is 5), then continuing with the quotient. Students who jump to larger primes without a systematic approach tend to get stuck. Q5 rewards the insight that the smallest number with n distinct prime factors is the product of the first n primes.

periods.activity_title: Last Digits and Divisibility: Deriving Tests for 2, 5, and 10

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remainders when 78, 99, 173, 572, 980, 1111, 2345 are each divided by (a) 10, (b) 5, (c) 2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore whether each statement is always, sometimes, or never true: (a) sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4; (b) sum of two odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to list the first 15 multiples of 10, then circle just the units digit of each. Ask: what do you notice? Repeat for multiples of 5, then multiples of 2. Students record the pattern (units digit 0 for 10; units digit 0 or 5 for 5; units digit 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 for 2) and state each rule as a divisibility test in their own words.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126 ("find the remainders when 78, 99, 173, 572, 980, 1111, 2345 are each divided by (a) 10, (b) 5, (c) 2…."). Rather than dividing each number fully, they apply the last-digit rules they derived to find remainders without long division and verify a few by actual division.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q3, section 5.5 p.125 ("explore whether each statement is always, sometimes, or never true: (a) sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4; (b) sum of two odd numbers is a multiple of 4…."). Students test specific cases and then try to identify when each statement holds or fails, writing a brief explanation.

Quick debrief: students state the three rules (for 2, 5, 10) and the class verifies the Q3 conclusions together. Note that the remainder when any number is divided by 10 is simply its units digit — a useful quick-check that applies across many contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who know the divisibility rules by rote often cannot explain why they work; the opening list-and-observe sequence makes the last-digit pattern the students' own discovery rather than a handed-down fact. For Q3, the answer is 'sometimes' for both parts — students who test only one case and generalise should be asked for a counterexample.

periods.activity_title: Last Two and Three Digits: Deriving Tests for 4 and 8

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: 2024 is a leap year. Leap years are multiples of 4, except multiples of 100 that are not multiples of 400. (a) From your birth year to now, which years were leap years? (b) From 2024 to 2099, how many leap years are there?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the largest and smallest 4-digit numbers that are both divisible by 4 and palindromes.

time_bands.activity: Pose the puzzle from section 5.5: 12 and 22 share the same units digit (2), yet only 12 is divisible by 4. Ask students to investigate — what additional digit(s) must we look at? Students list two-digit multiples of 4 (04, 08, 12, 16, … 96) and compare with non-multiples having the same units digit. They conclude that the last two digits together determine divisibility by 4.

Extend the investigation to 8 using the same approach: list three-digit multiples of 8 (008, 016, … 992) and observe that the last three digits determine divisibility by 8. Ask: why does one more prime factor of 2 require checking one more digit? State both rules clearly on the board.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.5 p.125 ("2024 is a leap year; leap years are multiples of 4 except multiples of 100 that are not multiples of 400; from your birth year to now, which years were leap years?…") applying the divisibility-by-4 rule in a real-world context.

Students begin Figure it Out Q2, section 5.5 p.125 ("find the largest and smallest 4-digit palindromes divisible by 4…."). Students identify what a 4-digit palindrome looks like (abba form) and apply the last-two-digit rule to the 'ba' part.

periods.teacher_notes: The insight that divisibility by 4 depends only on the last two digits (not the whole number) is often surprising; anchoring it to the fact that 100 is already divisible by 4 helps — any number's value above the last two digits is automatically a multiple of 4. For the palindrome problem, students who try exhaustive search should be steered toward using the palindrome structure to constrain the possibilities.

periods.activity_title: Applying All Five Divisibility Tests Together

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: The teacher asked if 14560 is divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10. Guna checked only two of these numbers and declared divisibility by all. What could those two numbers be?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of 572, 2352, 5600, 6000, 77622160 are divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write two numbers whose product is 10000, where neither number has 0 as its units digit.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 5.5 p.126 ("the teacher asked if 14560 is divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10; Guna checked only two of these numbers and declared divisibility by all; what could those two numbers be?…"). Students must reason about which divisibility tests imply others — for example, divisibility by 8 implies divisibility by 4 and by 2.

Students solve Figure it Out Q6, section 5.5 p.126 ("which of 572, 2352, 5600, 6000, 77622160 are divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10?…"), applying all five tests to each number. For the large number 77622160, they use only last-digit and last-three-digit checks, demonstrating the power of the rules.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q7, section 5.5 p.126 ("write two numbers whose product is 10000, where neither number has 0 as its units digit…."). Students use prime factorisation of 10000 = 2⁴ × 5⁴ to split the factors, then verify that neither number ends in 0.

Debrief Q5: which pair of tests from {2, 4, 5, 8, 10} is the minimal sufficient set, and why? Students articulate the implication chain. This closing argument consolidates the section's reasoning into a single memorable principle.

periods.teacher_notes: Q5 is the richest reasoning item in the section: the key insight is that checking divisibility by 8 and by 5 is sufficient, since 8 implies 4 and 2, while 5 together with 2 implies 10. Students who list all five tests for Q6 rather than identifying the minimal set have not yet grasped this implication structure — a targeted question to those students helps.

periods.activity_title: Special Numbers: What Makes Each One Unique?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk (Special Numbers), section 5.6 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: In each box of four numbers, explain how each number is special compared to the others. Share and compare reasons with classmates. Boxes include: {9, 16, 25, 43}; {5, 7, 3, 8}; {27, 3, 17, 27}; {12, 35, 11, 24}; {123, 31, 44, 65}.

time_bands.activity: Pose the first box {9, 16, 25, 43} from Math Talk (Special Numbers), section 5.6 p.126 ("in each box of four numbers, explain how each number is special compared to the others…."). Ask students to work silently and note what property of each number sets it apart. Collect two or three responses for 43 — draw out that it can be 'special' as the only prime or as the only non-perfect-square.

Small groups of three or four each take one of the remaining boxes ({5, 7, 3, 8}; {27, 3, 17, 27}; {12, 35, 11, 24}; {123, 31, 44, 65}) and brainstorm as many valid 'special' reasons as possible for each number in their box, writing them in their notebooks. Encourage groups to use prime factorisation, divisibility tests, and properties from the chapter.

Each group presents one box to the class. After each presentation, the class is invited to add further valid reasons the presenting group did not find. The teacher records on the board when two students give different valid reasons for the same number being special.

Whole-class reflection: can a number be special for contradictory reasons in different comparisons? Discuss briefly — 8 might be the only even number in one box but the only power of 2 in another, showing that 'special' is always relative to the comparison group.

periods.teacher_notes: The open-ended nature of this activity means there is no single correct answer; resist the urge to validate one reason and move on — multiple valid reasons for the same number are the point. A common limitation is that students draw only on the current chapter's vocabulary; prompt them to also use vocabulary from earlier chapters (square numbers, even/odd, multiples) to surface richer arguments.

periods.activity_title: Prime Puzzle: Filling Grids with Prime Factors

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk (Prime Puzzle), section 5.6 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill grids with prime numbers so that the product of each row equals the number to its right and the product of each column equals the number below it. Two grids provided (3×3 and larger). Sub-parts: (a) solve the first puzzle; (b) solve the second larger puzzle.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Prime Puzzle from Math Talk (Prime Puzzle), section 5.6 p.127 ("fill grids with prime numbers so that the product of each row equals the number to its right and the product of each column equals the number below it…."). With the class, perform prime factorisations of all the row and column products given in the first (3×3) grid, writing the factor lists on the board.

Students work individually or in pairs on sub-part (a) — solving the 3×3 grid. The strategy is to match prime factors from the row and column product lists simultaneously. Teacher circulates asking: which prime must appear in this cell? Why can it not be a composite?

Students who complete the 3×3 puzzle move to sub-part (b) — the larger grid. This requires managing more simultaneous constraints. Students who are still working on (a) are encouraged to try a different arrangement if they reach a contradiction.

Class share: a volunteer fills in the 3×3 solution on the board. The class verifies by computing row and column products. If multiple valid solutions exist, note that uniqueness is not guaranteed — a brief discussion of whether the puzzle has one or many solutions is a fitting close.

periods.teacher_notes: The Prime Puzzle is a constraint-satisfaction problem; students who try to fill cells randomly will struggle, while those who factorise the row/column products first and allocate prime factors systematically will succeed. A common error is placing a composite number in a cell — each cell must contain a prime, and that constraint should be checked against every trial placement.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Consolidation: Mixed Problem-Solving Across Number Properties

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of all numbers from 1 to 10, except 7. (Try This)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of all the numbers from 1 to 10. (Try This)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.110
textbook_items_in_class.description: Who am I? (a) A number less than 40, one factor is 7, digit sum is 8. (b) A number less than 100, two factors are 3 and 5, one digit is 1 more than the other.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find any three numbers that are multiples of 25 but not multiples of 50.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.111 ("find the smallest number that is a multiple of all numbers from 1 to 10, except 7….") and Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.111 ("find the smallest number that is a multiple of all the numbers from 1 to 10…."). The strategy is prime factorisation of each number from 1 to 10, then taking the highest power of each prime that appears.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.110 ("who am I? (a) a number less than 40, one factor is 7, digit sum is 8; (b) a number less than 100, two factors are 3 and 5, one digit is 1 more than the other…."). These riddles integrate factor reasoning with digit properties, drawing on divisibility knowledge from section 5.5.

Students solve Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.111 ("find any three numbers that are multiples of 25 but not multiples of 50…."). Students reason that multiples of 25 that are not multiples of 50 are odd multiples of 25 — they verify with divisibility by 2.

Class debrief on the 'LCM of 1 to 10' problem: students share their prime factorisation approach. Connect back to the chapter's central idea — prime factorisation reveals the structure of every number, making problems about multiples, factors, and divisibility tractable.

periods.teacher_notes: For Q9 and Q10, the prime factorisation approach (take the highest power of each prime up to 10) is elegant but students may not see it immediately; prompt them by asking: what must the number contain as a factor to be divisible by 8? By 9? These are the bridging questions. The 'Who am I?' riddles reward students who check all multiples of 7 less than 40 for a digit sum of 8, rather than guessing.

periods.activity_title: Open Problems and Creative Reasoning in Prime Time

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many three-digit prime numbers can you make using each of 2, 4 and 5 exactly once?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: 3 is prime and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also prime. Find at least five other primes p for which 2p + 1 is also prime.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers?

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.115 ("how many three-digit prime numbers can you make using each of 2, 4 and 5 exactly once?…"). Students list all six permutations of {2, 4, 5}, eliminate those divisible by 2 or 5 by inspection (using divisibility rules from section 5.5), and test the remaining candidates for primality.

Students extend their investigation from an earlier unit's Q12 work into a fresh exploration: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115 ("3 is prime and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also prime; find at least five other primes p for which 2p + 1 is also prime…."). Students compile their own list of such primes, looking for patterns in which primes qualify.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115 ("which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers?…"). Students factorise each candidate and count distinct prime factors, distinguishing 'distinct' from 'with multiplicity'.

Chapter close: students write one sentence each — 'The most surprising thing I discovered about prime numbers is…' — and share with the group. The teacher draws out two or three key ideas from the chapter (primes as atoms of multiplication, uniqueness of factorisation, divisibility rules as shortcuts) without re-teaching them.

periods.teacher_notes: For Q11, the divisibility tests from section 5.5 eliminate four of the six permutations immediately (even units digit or units digit 5), leaving only 245 and 425 — and both of these are also composite, so the answer is zero three-digit primes, a surprising result worth a class discussion. Q10 requires attention to the word 'distinct' — 45 = 3² × 5 has only two distinct prime factors, not three.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30. A player says 'idli-vada' at numbers that are common multiples of both 3 and 5. 30 = 3 × 10 = 5 × 6, so it is divisible by both. 21 is divisible by 3 but not 5; 25 is divisible by 5 but not 3; 35 is divisible by 5 but not 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 3 and multiples of 5 and identify the number that appears in both lists.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises a multiple of 3 but does not check divisibility by 5, confusing 'idli' with 'idli-vada'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recognises a multiple of 5 but does not check divisibility by 3, confusing 'vada' with 'idli-vada'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises a multiple of 5 but does not check divisibility by 3, perhaps drawn to 35 because it ends in 5.

items.prompt: A number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Which of the following correctly classifies the numbers 1, 13, and 15?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 is prime; 13 is prime; 15 is composite

options.label: B
options.text: 1 is neither prime nor composite; 13 is prime; 15 is composite

options.label: C
options.text: 1 is prime; 13 is prime; 15 is prime

options.label: D
options.text: 1 is composite; 13 is prime; 15 is composite

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 is neither prime nor composite (it has only one factor, itself); 13 is prime (factors: 1 and 13 only); 15 is composite (factors: 1, 3, 5, 15).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: prime numbers have exactly two factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor and is classified separately.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student classifies 1 as prime, a common misconception arising from 1 being only divisible by 1 and itself (without recognising that 'itself' and '1' are the same number, leaving only one factor).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student classifies 1 as prime and 15 as prime, failing to factor 15 = 3 × 5 and misapplying the definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student classifies 1 as composite, perhaps confusing 'not prime' with 'composite', without recognising the special status of 1.

inclusivity.support: Write out all the factors of 1, of 13, and of 15 separately and count them before classifying.
inclusivity.challenge: Give your own example of a two-digit composite number and list all its factors to confirm it is composite.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may not have checked all common factors of 12 and 16, perhaps noting they are both even but stopping before finding 4 as a common factor.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'There must be at least one prime between any two consecutive multiples of 10 (for example, between 20 and 30, between 30 and 40, and so on).' Is this claim true or false? Justify your answer with evidence from the primes up to 100.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The claim is true for all decades up to 100. In each group of ten consecutive integers (21–30, 31–40, 41–50, 51–60, 61–70, 71–80, 81–90, 91–100) at least one prime exists. For example: 23 and 29 lie in 21–30; 31 and 37 in 31–40; 41 and 43 in 41–50; 53 and 59 in 51–60; 61 and 67 in 61–70; 71 and 73 in 71–80; 83 and 89 in 81–90; 97 in 91–100. The claim holds for all decades in the range examined, though it is not guaranteed to hold for arbitrarily large decades (there exist arbitrarily long runs of composites).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the completed Sieve of Eratosthenes to identify at least one prime in each decade from 1–10 through 91–100.

inclusivity.support: Look at your sieve row by row and write down the primes in each decade before deciding whether the claim holds.
inclusivity.challenge: Suppose the claim were extended beyond 100 — can you think of a reason why very long stretches of consecutive composite numbers must eventually occur?

items.prompt: Anshu writes 72 = 8 × 9 and Guna writes 72 = 2 × 36. They both claim to have factorised 72. Explain why neither factorisation is a prime factorisation, then write the correct prime factorisation of 72. Using the prime factorisation, determine whether 72 and 35 share any common prime factor.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Neither 8 × 9 nor 2 × 36 is a prime factorisation because both contain composite factors (8, 9, 36 are all composite). The prime factorisation of 72 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, written as 2³ × 3². The prime factorisation of 35 is 5 × 7. Comparing the two lists — {2, 3} for 72 and {5, 7} for 35 — reveals no shared prime factor, so 72 and 35are co-prime.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Continue breaking each composite factor until only primes remain, then compare the two prime factor lists to check for shared primes.

inclusivity.support: Draw a factor tree for 72 starting with 8 × 9, then break each of 8 and 9 further until you reach only prime numbers at the branch ends.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a different factor tree for 72 starting with a different first split, and confirm that you reach the same set of prime factors — explaining why the set must always be the same.

items.prompt: Two numbers have prime factorisations 2² × 3 × 5 and 3² × 7. Without computing their product or any other multiplication, determine: (a) whether the two numbers are co-prime, and (b) whether the first number divides the second. Justify each answer using the prime factorisation method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The two numbers are NOT co-prime. Their prime factor lists are {2, 3, 5} and {3, 7}; the prime 3 appears in both, so their greatest common factor is at least 3, which is greater than 1. (b) The first number does NOT divide the second. For the first to divide the second, the prime factorisation of the first (2² × 3 × 5) would need to be fully contained in that of the second (3² × 7). The prime 2 appears in the first but not at all in the second, so the containment fails.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the prime factor lists for shared primes (co-primality) and check whether every prime in the first list appears at least as many times in the second list (divisibility).

inclusivity.support: Write the prime factors of each number as a list and use a diagram or colour-coding to find primes that appear in both lists.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one prime factor in the second number so that the first number does divide the second, and show that your change works.

items.prompt: A student says: 'To find the remainder when a number is divided by 5, I only need to look at the units digit.' Explain why this rule works, and use it to find the remainder when 2347 is divided by 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The rule works because every multiple of 10 ends in 0 and is therefore divisible by 5 with remainder 0. Any number can be split into its tens-and-above part (which is always a multiple of 10, and hence divisible by 5) and its units digit. The remainder when the whole number is divided by 5 is therefore equal to the remainder when just the units digit is divided by 5. For 2347: units digit is 7; 7 divided by 5 gives remainder 2. So the remainder is 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Observe that the tens-and-above part of any number is a multiple of 10 (hence of 5), leaving only the units digit to determine the remainder on division by 5.

inclusivity.support: Write 2347 as 2340 + 7, check that 2340 is divisible by 5, and then divide only 7 by 5 to find the remainder.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain why the same kind of reasoning gives the remainder on division by 10, and state what extra information you would need to find the remainder on division by 4.

items.prompt: The divisibility test for 4 says: a number is divisible by 4 if and only if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. Explain why looking at only the last one digit is insufficient for divisibility by 4, giving a concrete pair of numbers that shows this. Then apply the last-two-digit test to determine whether 3916 is divisible by 4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One digit is insufficient because two numbers can share the same units digit yet only one is divisible by 4. Example: 12 and 22 both end in 2, but 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (divisible) while 22 ÷ 4 = 5 remainder 2 (not divisible). The reason is that 100 is divisible by 4 (100 = 4 × 25), so any number's hundreds-and-above portion is always a multiple of 4; the remainder on division by 4 depends entirely on the last two digits. For 3916: last two digits are 16; 16 ÷ 4 = 4 with no remainder. Therefore 3916 is divisible by 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Note that 100 is divisible by 4, so only the last two digits determine the remainder; check whether those two digits form a multiple of 4.

inclusivity.support: Try dividing each of 12, 22, 32, 42, 52 by 4 and see which ones are divisible — then notice what the last two digits of the divisible ones have in common.
inclusivity.challenge: Use similar reasoning to explain why the last three digits determine divisibility by 8, and verify your explanation with one example.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 60: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60. Common factors of 24 and 60: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. items.prompt: A thread is wound around a circle with 10 pegs, with a gap of 3 pegs between each step (so the thread goes from peg 1 to peg 4 to peg 7, and so on). Predict whether the thread will visit all 10 pegs before returning to peg 1, and explain your prediction using the idea of co-prime numbers. Verify by listing the pegs visited in order.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Since 10 and 3 are co-prime (their only common factor is 1 — factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10; factors of 3: 1, 3; common factor is only 1), the thread will visit all 10 pegs exactly once before returning to the start. Pegs visited in order (starting from peg 1, adding 3 each time modulo 10): 1, 4, 7, 10, 3, 6, 9, 2, 5, 8, 1. All 10 pegs are visited.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the peg count and gap are co-prime; if so, every peg is visited before the thread returns to its start.

items.prompt: Using prime factorisation, determine whether 180 is divisible by 12, and whether 180 is divisible by 48. Show all working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Prime factorisation of 180: 180 = 2 × 90 = 2 × 2 × 45 = 2 × 2 × 9 × 5 = 2² × 3² × 5. Prime factorisation of 12: 12 = 2² × 3. Every prime factor of 12 (two 2s and one 3) appears in the factorisation of 180 (two 2s and two 3s), so 180 is divisible by 12 (180 ÷ 12 = 15). Prime factorisation of 48: 48 = 2⁴ × 3. 48 requires four 2s, but 180 has only two 2s, so the factorisation of 48 is NOT contained in that of 180. Therefore 180 is not divisible by 48.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare prime factorisations: the divisor divides the dividend if and only if each prime appears at least as many times in the dividend's factorisation as in the divisor's.

inclusivity.support: Write out the factor trees for 180, 12, and 48 separately, list the prime factors of each, and then compare the lists for 12 and 180, and for 48 and 180.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the largest number that divides 180 by identifying all possible divisors whose prime factorisations are contained in that of 180.

items.prompt: Find three prime numbers, each less than 20, whose product is 374. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Begin by checking small primes. 374 is even, so 2 divides it: 374 ÷ 2 = 187. Check whether 187 is prime: 187 ÷ 11 = 17. So 187 = 11 × 17. Therefore 374 = 2 × 11 × 17. All three factors (2, 11, 17) are prime and less than 20. The three prime numbers are 2, 11, and 17.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Systematically divide by small primes in order to find the complete prime factorisation of 374.

inclusivity.challenge: Verify your answer by multiplying your three primes together and confirming the product is 374, then explain why there cannot be any other set of three primes less than 20 with the same product.

items.prompt: A teacher asks whether 13720 is divisible by each of 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10. A clever student says she only needs to check two of these five numbers and can then answer for all five. Which two numbers should she check, and what will her answers be for all five?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student should check divisibility by 8 and by 5 (or equivalently by 8 and 10). Checking 8: last three digits of 13720 are 720; 720 ÷ 8 = 90, so 13720 is divisible by 8. Since 8 = 2³, divisibility by 8 implies divisibility by 4 (= 2²) and by 2. Checking 5: units digit of 13720 is 0, which is 0 or 5, so 13720 is divisible by 5. Divisibility by both 2 and 5 implies divisibility by 10. Answers: 13720 is divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that divisibility by 8 implies divisibility by 4 and 2, and that divisibility by 10 follows from divisibility by both 2 and 5; check only 8 and 5 (or 8 and 10) to certify all five.

inclusivity.support: Apply each divisibility test (last digit for 2, 5, 10; last two digits for 4; last three digits for 8) to 13720 one at a time and record your results before reasoning about which tests imply others.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain in a full sentence why checking divisibility by 8 alone is enough to conclude divisibility by both 4 and 2, using the relationship between 2, 4, and 8 as powers of 2.

items.prompt: In a Prime Puzzle, a 2×2 grid must be filled with prime numbers so that the product of the first row equals 21, the product of the second row equals 22, the product of the first column equals 14, and the product of the second column equals 33. Find the four prime numbers that fill the grid.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Factorise each constraint: row 1 product = 21 = 3 × 7; row 2 product = 22 = 2 × 11; col 1 product = 14 = 2 × 7; col 2 product = 33 = 3 × 11. The cell in row 1, col 1 must divide both 21 and 14; the common prime factor is 7. So cell (1,1) = 7. Then cell (1,2) = 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Cell (2,1) = 14 ÷ 7 = 2. Cell (2,2) = 22 ÷ 2 = 11. Verify: col 2 = 3 × 11 = 33. All four cells contain primes: 7, 3, 2, 11.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Factorise each row and column product into primes, then allocate primes to cells by matching row and column constraints simultaneously.

inclusivity.support: Write the prime factorisation of 21, 22, 14, and 33 separately, then ask: which prime must be in the top-left cell because it appears in both the first row product and the first column product?

items.prompt: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of every whole number from 1 to 6 (inclusive). Show your working using prime factorisations.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The required number must be divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Prime factorisations: 1 = (no prime factors); 2 = 2; 3 = 3; 4 = 2²; 5 = 5; 6 = 2 × 3. The smallest such number contains each prime to the highest power appearing across these factorisations: 2² (from 4), 3¹ (from 3 or 6), 5¹ (from 5). Smallest number = 2² × 3 × 5 = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the prime factorisation of each number from 1 to 6, then take the highest power of each prime that appears; the product is the smallest common multiple.

items.prompt: List all the three-digit numbers that can be formed using the digits 1, 3, and 7 (each used exactly once) and determine which of them are prime. Show how you used divisibility rules to eliminate non-primes before checking the remaining candidates.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The six permutations of {1, 3, 7} are: 137, 173, 317, 371, 713, 731. Divisibility checks: all six end in an odd digit (1, 3, or 7), so none is divisible by 2. None ends in 0 or 5, so none is divisible by 5. Check remaining for primality by trial division up to their square roots (√731 < 28, so test primes up to 27: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23). 137: not divisible by 3 (1+3+7=11), 7 (137÷7≈19.6), 11 (137÷11≈12.5) — prime. 173: not divisible by 3 (1+7+3=11), 7, 11, 13 — prime. 317: digit sum 11, not divisible by 7, 11, 13, 17 — prime. 371 = 7 × 53 — composite. 713 = 23 × 31 — composite. 731 = 17 × 43 — composite. Prime three-digit numbers: 137, 173, 317.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all permutations, use last-digit divisibility rules to eliminate multiples of 2 and 5, then test remaining numbers for primality by trial division up to the square root.

inclusivity.support: First write all six three-digit numbers formed by 1, 3, 7. Check each: does it end in an even digit? Does it end in 0 or 5? If neither, try dividing it by 7, 11, 13, 17, 23 to see if any division is exact.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain why you do not need to test divisors larger than 27 when checking whether any of these six numbers is prime.
